learn.title: Input before the program starts
learn.body: You can give a program words on the command line: `./greet Ada`. C passes them to `main` if you write it as `int main(int argc, char *argv[])`. Now the program can be told what to do when it starts.

learn.title: What the two names hold
learn.body: `argc` counts the words, including the program name. `argv` is an array of strings, one per word. For `./greet Ada`, `argc` is 2, `argv[0]` is `"./greet"` and `argv[1]` is `"Ada"`.

learn.title: Use the argument
learn.body: If the count is not 2, it prints a usage line and returns 1, the sign of failure. Run as `./hello Ada` it prints `hello, Ada`.

learn.title: Spaces split words
learn.body: The shell splits the line at spaces. `./hello Ada Lovelace` gives `argc` 3. Quotes keep words together: `./hello "Ada Lovelace"` is one argument with `argc` 2.

learn.title: Arguments are text
learn.body: `argv[1]` is the string `"12"`, not a number. `atoi` from `stdlib.h` converts it to 12. It gives 0 for non-numbers and cannot tell you it failed.

learn.title: Check before you use
steps: Without arguments `argc` is 1, since the program name counts
`argv[1]` would then be missing, and reading it is undefined
So test `argc != 2` first and print a usage message
Return a nonzero value from `main` to report failure
